scenario: AITA for telling my father to fuck off for telling me I need to get my daughter into basketball? | I feel like I was too harsh and even my husband thinks I could have done it better but I feel like that's partly because he hasn't felt the full weight of my father's micromanagement. Growing up I had certain interests, I was VERY into these activities. Around the time I was in the 8th grade my sister got jealous of the success I was having in this area. After that point I was strongly "discouraged" from taking part in these activities unless it was at school. Instead they pushed me to work with children. They told me it was my gift (super Christian family) and that I shouldn't squander my talent. So there's the background on why I think I responded so strongly. My youngest daughter is tall and always has been. She's 11 years old and 5'6" and is still growing. Starting at about age 5? My father has pushed me to make her do basketball. Because she's tall, I mean let's ignore the fact that she inherited my clumsy gene, that she's a very shy girl, that she hates crowds and noise. Ugh. Anyway a few days ago I made a rare visit to my parent's house, I felt it was safe because family friends were there. I was bemoaning the utter lack of art day camps or just evening classes. All three of my girls love art so I'm looking for something that they will actually enjoy. My father brought up fucking basketball again. "You need to get youngest daughter into it, who cares if she doesn't want to. You're the parent just tell her she's doing it." Honestly it brought up a lot of really shitty feelings that I didn't realize were still hanging around. I got up grabbed my purse and told him he could fuck off and left. So reddit am I the asshole for my reaction here? Was I overreacting? I'm really torn here, I'm generally a people pleaser but I really don't think I was out of line and I'm certainly not going to apologize, because I'm not really sorry. Which makes me wonder if I'm an asshole for not apologizing.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I was being an asshole when I told my father to fuck off for telling me to get my daughter into basketball. Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, there's a lot of background here. I had certain interests growing up, and my sister got jealous of my success in those areas. Because of that jealousy, I was discouraged from pursuing those activities unless it was at school. Instead, my family pushed me towards working with children, saying it was my gift as part of a super Christian family. That's a lot to unpack. Now, with my own daughter, who is tall and has inherited some of my clumsy genes, she's also very shy and hates crowds and noise. Despite all this, my father keeps pushing me to get her into basketball because she's tall. He even went as far as saying, "You need to get your youngest daughter into it. Who cares if she doesn't want to? You're the parent just tell her she's doing it." That's when I snapped. I told him to fuck off and left. Now I'm wondering if I was being an asshole for reacting that way. Was I overreacting? I generally try to please people, but I don't think I was out of line, and I'm not sorry for what I did. But does that make me an asshole for not apologizing? Let me think about this step by step. First, I need to understand why I reacted the way I did. It seems like my father's pushiness triggered some deep-seated issues from my own childhood. I was discouraged from pursuing my interests because of my sister's jealousy, and now I'm seeing a similar pattern with my daughter. My father's advice feels like a repetition of the same kind of micromanagement I experienced growing up. On one hand, I can see why my father might think basketball is a good idea for my daughter because of her height. It's a common association, and he might be trying to help. But on the other hand, he's disregarding her personality and interests, which is something I was taught to value as part of a Christian upbringing focused on working with children. I also need to consider the dynamics between me and my father. There's a history of him pushing me into certain activities, and now he's doing the same with my daughter. This could be why I reacted so strongly. It's not just about the basketball; it's about feeling like my father is trying to control my daughter's life in the same way he controlled mine. Now, thinking about whether I was being an asshole. The term "asshole" is pretty strong, so I need to evaluate if my reaction was justified or if it crossed a line. I told my father to fuck off, which is a harsh way to express anger. While it's understandable that I was upset, the way I expressed it might have been excessive. However, I also need to consider the context. My father was being pushy and disregarding my daughter's feelings and interests. In that moment, I felt like I had to stand up for my daughter and protect her from the same kind of pressure I experienced as a child. That makes me feel like my reaction, while harsh, was born out of a desire to protect my daughter. But then, I also have to think about the consequences of my reaction. By telling my father to fuck off, I might have damaged our relationship further. It could have made it harder for us to communicate in the future, especially if I don't apologize. That's something to consider. I also mentioned that my husband thinks I could have handled it better. He hasn't felt the full weight of my father's micromanagement, so he might not fully understand why I reacted the way I did. That's a valid point. My husband's perspective is important, and I should take it into account, even if I don't agree with it entirely. Another thing to think about is whether I'm holding onto past hurts that are influencing my current behavior. The fact that this situation brought up a lot of "really shitty feelings" that I didn't realize were still around suggests that there's some unresolved emotional baggage. It might be helpful to address those feelings separately, perhaps through talking to a therapist or a trusted friend. I also need to consider the impact on my daughter. While I was standing up for her, the way I did it might have been more about my own feelings than her well-being. It's important to model healthy conflict resolution for her, so she can learn how to handle similar situations in the future. In terms of whether I'm an asshole for not apologizing, I have to weigh the importance of apologizing against my genuine feelings. If I'm not sorry for what I did, then apologizing just to keep the peace might not be authentic. However, relationships often require compromise and understanding, even if it means apologizing for the sake of the relationship. Overall, I think my reaction was understandable given the history and the emotions involved, but the way I expressed it might have been too harsh. It's a fine line between standing up for what I believe is right and maintaining respectful communication with family members. I also need to consider whether there's a middle ground. Could I have expressed my frustration without being so confrontational? Maybe I could have calmly explained why I don't think basketball is the right fit for my daughter, or suggested alternative activities that align more with her interests. In the end, I have to decide what's more important: protecting my daughter from what I perceive as harmful influence or maintaining a respectful and open relationship with my father. It's a tough choice, and there's no clear right or wrong answer. But understanding the reasons behind my reaction and considering the impact on all parties involved can help me make a more informed decision moving forward.
